library(tidyverse)
library(viridis)
library(ggridges)

Exercise 1

The data was collected by the American National Election Studies. The data collection for the study began in August 2020 and continued until November 2020. A sample of US eligible voters were surveyed. The sample randomly assigned to one of three groups: web only, mixed web and phone, and mixed video.

Exercise 3

ggplot(anes, aes(x = factor(ideology), fill = factor(ideology))) +
  geom_bar() +
  
  labs(x = "Ideology", y = "Number of voters", fill = "Ideology") +
  theme_minimal()

4 is the most common ideology. The two smallest bars are at the extreme ends of the plot, most respondents aren’t at ideological extremes and tend to be moderate. A considerable number of respondents didn’t disclose their ideology, which should be consiered when interpreting the visualization.

Exercise 4

ggplot(anes, aes(y = factor(ideology), fill = urbanrural)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  # scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  labs(x = "Proportion of voters",
       y = "Ideology",
       fill = "Type of location",
       title = "Location type by political ideology") +
  theme_minimal()

  • Suburb and small town have a considerable amount of respondents from each ideology and don’t seem to be dominated by a single one, which contrasts with the rural and urban respondents.

  • It’s easier to compare internal composition of ideology groups with proportions. If we were relying on counts, say on the city bar, the liberal cohort would swallow the other groups and it would be harder to make a comparison.

  • The proportion of N/A across the ideology bars is fairly consistent and doesn’t vary substantially by ideology.

Exercise 6

anes |>
  drop_na(hunt_fish, scientists) |>
  mutate(
    hunted_fished = if_else(
      hunt_fish == 0,
      "Did Not Hunt or Fish",
      "Hunted or Fished"
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hunted_fished, y = ideology, fill = hunted_fished)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Warmth Toward Scientists by Hunting/Fishing Status",
    x = "Hunting or Fishing Status",
    y = "Feeling Thermometer: Scientists (0–100)",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
Warning: Removed 1020 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_boxplot()`).

+Yes, the hunt/fish group is more dispersed and skews slightly cooler at the bottom.

Exercise 7

anes |>
  drop_na(hunt_fish, scientists) |>
  mutate(
    hunted_fished = if_else(hunt_fish == 0, "Did Not Hunt or Fish", "Hunted or Fished")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = ideology, y = hunted_fished, fill = hunted_fished)) +
  geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Warmth Toward Scientists by Hunting/Fishing Status",
    x = "Feeling Thermometer: Scientists (0–100)",
    y = NULL,
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
Picking joint bandwidth of 0.292

  • Both groups are scientist friendly as a whole, with the hunters and fishers being slightly more lukewarm. Both groups skew left.

Exercise 8

  • Both plots agree that hunters/fishers lean more conservative.
  • The five-number summary about the data is easier to see on the box plot. If we’re trying to determine which median is higher, the box plot is easier to glean from. +The ridge plots show the distributional shape far better than the compact boxes. So if we want to learn about the modality, skew and where most of the masses are, it’s the plot of choice.
  • I think the ridge plot is better suited to glean a more nuanced understanding from. Not only does it communicate the information that we could get from the boxplot, we also see a better visual of where most of the masses live. > YOUR COMMENTS HERE

Exercise 10

  • Is there a relationship between the type of place respondents reside and whether they’re into hunting/fishing?
  • hunt_fish and urbanrural
anes |>
  drop_na(hunt_fish, urbanrural) |>
  mutate(
    hunted_fished = if_else(hunt_fish == 0, "Did Not Hunt or Fish", "Hunted or Fished"),
    
    urbanrural = factor(urbanrural, levels = c("city", "suburb", "small town", "rural"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = urbanrural, fill = hunted_fished)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "Hunting/Fishing Participation by Type of Residence",
    x = "Type of Place",
    y = "Proportion",
    fill = NULL
  )

  • Since both are categorical variables, we’re interested in their counts. Also, since the number of respondents between the type of residence varies wildly, the proportion is ideal as we’re more interested about the binary within the population. It’s for this reason that a stacked, proportion-filled bar plot is the most ideal.

  • Unsurprisingly, the closer a person is to the city, the less likely to engage in hunting or fishing.
